issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident, 'Babies' as a salient auditory trigger is hard to connect clinically unless the accident specifically involved infants/crying, which is not supported by the rest of the profile. The other trigger items (intrusive thoughts, nightmare residue) are generic trauma reactivation cues, making this item stand out as trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Make sure never to be alone with another person' suggests avoidance linked to fear of being accused of harming someone or of interpersonal/sexual threat, which is not coherently supported by the accident trauma type, threat items, or appraisals. The rest of the profile is organized around generalized danger/vulnerability, not being alone with another person specifically.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel permanently humiliated by what happened' is not impossible after an accident, but here it lacks support from the other selected items. The threat and strategy items focus on physical danger and hypervigilance, while no memory or trigger content suggests shame-based social exposure. In this profile, humiliation is the least coherent appraisal and appears disconnected from the accident-focused formulation.

vignette:
Minh Tran was 33 when he came to treatment, a married Vietnamese American man who worked as a physical therapist in a busy outpatient rehabilitation clinic. The event he returned to again and again had happened more than a year earlier on an ordinary evening drive home. He had been stopped at an intersection when another vehicle came through at speed and struck the driver’s side of his car. He remembered the sound with particular force: the explosive crack of metal folding inward, glass breaking, the blunt percussion of the impact inside the enclosed space of the car. In the seconds that followed, he was aware of being pinned awkwardly, of pain shooting through his body, and of the terrifying uncertainty about whether he would be able to move properly or get out. He has described that moment less as a sequence than as a violent sensory imprint, with the noise of the crash standing out as something his mind still reacts to before he has time to think.

In the weeks afterward, Minh found that the accident did not stay in the past in any settled way. Unwanted thoughts intruded while he was driving, lying in bed, or trying to focus on charting at work. They arrived abruptly, as if the collision were about to happen again, and sometimes he woke from a nightmare with the emotional force of it still on him, disoriented and already tense before he was fully awake. On those mornings there was often a residue that clung to him for hours; he would move through breakfast with his wife half-absorbed, listening too closely to sounds outside, feeling as though his body had not quite understood that the danger was over.

Loud noises became especially potent. If a weight slammed to the floor in the clinic gym, if a treatment table banged unexpectedly against the wall, if a car backfired in the parking lot, Minh felt his whole body react at once. He startled visibly and then hated how immediate and involuntary it seemed. What frightened him most was not only the jolt itself, but what it seemed to prove. He had come to believe that his body had been permanently damaged by the accident, that something fundamental in it no longer worked reliably. As a physical therapist, he spent his days talking with patients about strength, healing, and bodily adaptation, yet privately he was increasingly certain that he could no longer trust his own body. A sudden increase in heart rate, a flinch, a sense of tension in his muscles—these experiences did not feel temporary to him. They felt like evidence.

Over time, his days became organized around trying to feel prepared and in control. He cleaned and organized repeatedly at home, straightening surfaces, aligning objects, wiping down the kitchen again after it was already clean. The ritual made sense to him in the moment; if things were in order, he felt less exposed. Before leaving the house or entering a new place, he often mentally rehearsed worst-case scenarios. He would picture an accident in traffic, a violent confrontation in a parking garage, a piece of equipment failing in the clinic, and then walk himself through what he would do. He told himself this was practical, the only responsible way to live once you understood how quickly disaster could happen.

The same vigilance followed him into his workday. In treatment rooms and the open gym, Minh constantly scanned his surroundings. He noticed metal poles, scissors, heavy exercise equipment, anything that could become a weapon or dangerous object. If a new patient’s family member entered abruptly or someone raised their voice at the front desk, part of his attention snapped toward them immediately. This left him struggling to concentrate during sessions and while documenting, which embarrassed him because precision was part of how he understood himself professionally. He became slower with notes and more easily thrown off in conversation, occasionally asking patients to repeat themselves because his mind had gone elsewhere, tracking a sound in the hallway or the clang of equipment nearby.

At home, these habits accumulated consequences. His wife saw how long it took him to settle at night, how often he checked locks, peered out windows, or got up to straighten things after saying he was coming to bed. He was less present with her, more likely to drift into tense silence after a sudden noise or a poor night’s sleep. Minh understood that she experienced him as distant, but he also felt that relaxing would be reckless. He had come to believe that you can never know who will harm you, and ordinary settings no longer felt ordinary to him.

He finally sought help after a morning in the clinic when a loud crash from a dropped piece of equipment made him jump so hard that he lost his place with a patient mid-instruction and could not easily recover his concentration. The incident stayed with him all day. It was not only humiliating; it sharpened his fear that the accident had left him altered in a lasting way. By the time he came in, he was hoping for some way to feel less on guard and less controlled by these reactions, but he was equally afraid that treatment might confirm what he already believed—that his body was no longer trustworthy and that the world had become permanently unsafe.
